title: Taxonomy of visual techniques
credit: Published by GoodGlyph Studio under CC BY 4.0. The structure draws on the traditions listed in foundations.
citation_note: Sources are given as pointers to the underlying research and practice. Check the exact reference before quoting any of them in published work.

levels.operation: What the image asks the viewer to do.
levels.domain: What the image works through to get there.
levels.technique: The specific mechanism that does the work.
levels.execution: References in your own library that use the technique: the evidence.

operations.name: Differentiate
operations.question: What is different here?
operations.definition: Make one thing stand out from everything around it. The viewer notices a difference before anything else.

operations.name: Group
operations.question: What belongs together?
operations.definition: Make separate things read as one set, family or system. The viewer sees units instead of pieces.

operations.name: Sequence
operations.question: Where do I look next?
operations.definition: Control the order of looking. The viewer is led first here, then there, then there.

operations.name: Infer
operations.question: What does this mean beyond what I see?
operations.definition: Make the viewer complete the meaning: a hidden shape, a metaphor, a reference, a missing moment. The idea is supplied by the viewer, not shown.

domains.name: Feature
domains.definition: Visible properties of marks: light and dark, hue, saturation, temperature, size, shape, texture, sharpness. Works before you start thinking.

domains.name: Space
domains.definition: Where things sit and how much room they get: position, emptiness, depth, overlap, framing, cropping.

domains.name: Gestalt
domains.definition: The rules the eye uses to organize parts into wholes: nearness, enclosure, connection, continuity, symmetry, completion. Named after the Gestalt psychologists who described them.

domains.name: Social
domains.definition: Our automatic reading of people: faces, eyes, gestures, bodies. We follow gazes and see faces whether we mean to or not.

domains.name: Semantic
domains.definition: What the things in the image are and what they mean, and what happens when meanings are paired, merged or swapped.

domains.name: Cultural
domains.definition: Shared references the viewer brings: genres, famous images, learned symbols, reading direction, the look of how things are made.

domains.name: Time
domains.definition: Change across frames, or movement implied in a still: animation, motion graphics, comics and manga panels, images that hold several moments.

domains.name: Encoding
domains.definition: Data mapped onto visual variables such as position, length, color and count, in charts, maps and diagrams.

labeling_rules: Label the mechanism the image depends on. Test: if you removed it, would the image stop working? If not, don't label it.
Give 0 to 3 techniques per reference; most get 1 or 2. 'None' is a valid and useful answer for plain screenshots, documentation photos, and references saved for one small detail.
Every photo has some light and dark and every layout has some size differences. Label chiaroscuro or size hierarchy only when that contrast is the idea.

When two techniques fit the same element, use their 'Not to confuse with' notes to pick one. One element may carry two labels only when it does two different jobs (a sheer veil both hides and tints what's behind it: occlusion and transparency; a neon sign is both the light in the scene and the words that fix its meaning: glow and anchorage), never for two readings of the same job. When a newer technique names exactly the job an older label describes on the same element (a figure seen from behind: viewer stand-in, not gaze cue), keep only the more exact one.

For collages, grids and moodboards, label the technique of the arrangement (repetition, similarity, color blocking). If one idea carries the board (the flower-iris eye in a brand identity, a mark repeated on every tile), label that too, as a second label. A designed system (a brand board, a product family built to match) counts as similarity; a board of unrelated pieces collected for mood is 'none' unless its arrangement or one standout piece has an idea of its own.
Name the carrier: the specific element doing the work, in a few words ("the single lit face against black").
Pick the path that matches how this image uses the technique. Most images use the first path listed.
Confidence: 0.9 obvious and central; 0.7 clearly present and doing work; 0.5 a real supporting mechanism you would defend, not a faint presence. If you hesitate to defend it, leave it out.
Never label aesthetics, styles or subjects (Y2K, brutalism, cyberpunk, minimal). Those belong in the description and tags.

For video you see one poster frame. Label what the frame shows. Use Time techniques only when the frame itself shows them (trails, a staged beat) or the description states the motion plainly; motion it only guesses at ('likely', 'probably') doesn't count.

Describe how the image looks in the four look fields (medium, camera angle, framing, lighting), choosing each answer from its fixed list. They describe the look; techniques describe the mechanism. A low camera is always noted as an angle, and labeled viewpoint only when the angle is what the image depends on.
brief_method: Read the brief for what it needs the viewer to do, and name the operation (sometimes two).
Choose the domain to work through. The material often decides: a photo shoot works through Feature and Space, a campaign line through Semantic, a chart through Encoding.
Pick two or three candidate techniques. Say why each fits and what it would look like in this job.
Pull references from your own library that execute them and look at them before designing.
Design. Cite the technique and the reference numbers behind each decision.
Record the path (brief, techniques chosen and why, techniques rejected and why) so the reasoning can be reviewed later.

techniques.name: Chiaroscuro
techniques.definition: Strong light against deep shadow. The lit part becomes the subject and the dark swallows everything else.
techniques.why: The eye lands first on the strongest local contrast of light and dark, and darkness removes competing detail.
techniques.spot: Large areas near black, one directional light, the subject modeled by light rather than by outline.
techniques.use_when: Drama, gravity, intimacy, or one subject pulled out of a busy world.
techniques.fails_when: Light is spread evenly or the shadows go muddy gray, so nothing is singled out.
techniques.distinct: A silhouette is a flat dark shape with no interior; rim light is a thin bright edge from behind; glow is light that seems to come from the thing itself. Chiaroscuro models form with light falling on it. Tie-breaker with chiaroscuro and glow: when the light comes from a direction and models the form, it is chiaroscuro; when the figure is the brightest thing in the picture with no visible source, it is glow.
techniques.foundation: Baroque tenebrism (Caravaggio); Itten's contrast of light and dark, The Art of Color (1961)

techniques.name: Rim light
techniques.definition: A thin line of light around the subject's edge, usually from behind, that separates it from a dark background.
techniques.why: The bright outline defines the shape even when the front of the subject is in shadow.
techniques.spot: A glowing edge on hair, shoulders or the contour of an object, with the light coming from behind.
techniques.use_when: A dark subject must still read on a dark ground; cinematic, nocturnal or premium product moods.
techniques.fails_when: The rim is the only light and the subject reads as a cutout, or the background is light and the rim disappears.
techniques.foundation: Studio photography and film lighting: the back light of three-point lighting
techniques.distinct: A thin bright edge from behind. A broad soft halo around the subject is glow.

techniques.name: Silhouette
techniques.definition: The subject reduced to a solid shape against a contrasting ground, recognized by its outline alone.
techniques.why: We recognize things from their contour, so removing interior detail makes the outline carry the whole message.
techniques.spot: A flat dark (or light) shape with no interior detail and a clear, readable edge.
techniques.use_when: Iconic, instantly recognizable forms; mystery; reading from far away.
techniques.fails_when: Limbs or objects merge into one blob, so the outline stops being readable.
techniques.distinct: Chiaroscuro keeps the form modeled by light; a silhouette is flat.
techniques.foundation: Profile silhouette portraits (18th century, named after Étienne de Silhouette); Rubin on figure and ground (1915)

techniques.name: Pop-out
techniques.definition: Many similar items and one that differs in a single property, so it is found instantly.
techniques.why: A difference in one simple feature (color, tilt, size) is spotted before deliberate looking, across the whole field at once.
techniques.spot: A field of near-identical things with one odd one out.
techniques.use_when: Find-the-one ideas: the different product, the outlier, the rebel in the crowd.
techniques.fails_when: The odd one is defined only by a combination of features that each also appear in the crowd (a red circle among red squares and green circles); then it has to be searched for instead of popping out.
techniques.distinct: If the odd one differs in a feature (color, size, shape), it's pop-out; if it breaks the arrangement (lifted, rotated, out of line, a different kind of thing), it's a pattern break. When both, label the stronger. A saturation accent needs no crowd, just one vivid color in a muted image.
techniques.foundation: Treisman & Gelade, feature integration theory (1980)

techniques.name: Saturation accent
techniques.definition: One vivid, saturated color inside an otherwise muted or gray image: one element (even a single element in several hues), or a few small accents of the same hue.
techniques.why: With everything else quiet, the only intense color takes all the attention.
techniques.spot: A desaturated or monochrome scene with one element in full color, like a red coat in a gray street.
techniques.use_when: Singling out a product, a person or a detail while keeping the setting visible.
techniques.fails_when: Several elements are saturated, or the accent color repeats elsewhere and dilutes it.
techniques.distinct: Highlight and mute is the same move inside a chart or text. Tie-breaker for the color techniques. Saturation accent: one vivid element (one hue, a few small accents of the same hue, or a single multicolored element) in an otherwise muted or gray image. Pop-out needs a crowd of similar items with one odd one; saturation accent needs only a muted image. Warm–cool split: temperature separates subject from setting, whichever side is the warm one (a cool figure on a hot red field counts). Complementary pairing: two opposite hues together carry the image, usually one dominant and one in a smaller share. Value accent is the same move made with lightness instead of color.
techniques.foundation: Itten's contrast of saturation, The Art of Color (1961)

techniques.name: Warm–cool split
techniques.definition: Warm colors set against cool ones to separate subject from setting, or one zone from another.
techniques.why: Warm hues seem to come forward and cool ones to fall back, so temperature alone can create figure and depth.
techniques.spot: Orange skin against a teal background, a warm lamp in a blue room, a frame split into a warm and a cool half.
techniques.use_when: Separating subject from setting without light-dark contrast; night scenes; two opposing camps.
techniques.fails_when: It is applied as a default color grade with no reason, or warm and cool mix in both zones.
techniques.foundation: Itten's contrast of warm and cool, The Art of Color (1961)
techniques.distinct: Tie-breaker for the color techniques. Saturation accent: one vivid hue (one element, or a few small accents of the same hue) in an otherwise muted or gray image. Warm–cool split: temperature separates subject from setting, whichever side is the warm one (a cool figure on a hot red field counts). Complementary pairing: two opposite hues together carry the image, usually one dominant and one in a smaller share.

techniques.name: Complementary pairing
techniques.definition: Two opposite hues (red and green, blue and orange, yellow and violet) built into the image so each makes the other more intense, usually one dominant and one in a smaller share.
techniques.why: Opposite hues give the strongest hue contrast, and each looks more saturated next to the other.
techniques.spot: The image is carried by two dominant opposite colors.
techniques.use_when: Maximum vibrancy; a bold poster; a product set against its complementary color.
techniques.fails_when: Both colors take equal space and fight, so edges vibrate and nothing dominates. Give one a small share.
techniques.foundation: Chevreul, De la loi du contraste simultané des couleurs (1839); Itten's complementary contrast (1961)
techniques.distinct: Tie-breaker for the color techniques. Saturation accent: one vivid hue (one element, or a few small accents of the same hue) in an otherwise muted or gray image. Warm–cool split: temperature separates subject from setting, whichever side is the warm one (a cool figure on a hot red field counts). Complementary pairing: two opposite hues together carry the image, usually one dominant and one in a smaller share.

techniques.name: Simultaneous contrast
techniques.definition: Surrounding colors change how a color looks: the same gray reads warm on blue and cool on orange, light on black and dark on white. The image is built on that interaction.
techniques.why: We judge color and lightness relative to their surroundings, never in isolation.
techniques.spot: Colors that only make sense together; one color that seems to glow or shift because of what surrounds it.
techniques.use_when: Making a small palette feel rich; making one color glow by choosing its surroundings; optical play.
techniques.fails_when: It happens by accident: a brand color shifts on a new background and looks wrong.
techniques.foundation: Chevreul (1839); Albers, Interaction of Color (1963)

techniques.name: Scale disparity
techniques.definition: An extreme difference in size between elements, so the giant or the tiny one runs the image.
techniques.why: Size difference is read instantly, and it tells a story: power and smallness, ambition and vulnerability.
techniques.spot: A tiny figure next to a huge object, or one element vastly bigger than everything else.
techniques.use_when: Showing power, loneliness, ambition, or how much one thing matters.
techniques.fails_when: The sizes differ only a little, which reads as a mistake rather than an idea.
techniques.distinct: Size hierarchy grades sizes to set a reading order; scale disparity uses one extreme gap to make a point.
techniques.foundation: Arnheim, Art and Visual Perception (1954), on visual weight

techniques.name: Texture against flat
techniques.definition: A richly textured element set against a smooth, flat field, or a flat shape against a busy textured one, so the change of texture separates subject from ground.
techniques.why: A change of texture splits the image into figure and ground before anything else is read.
techniques.spot: Fur, crumpled paper, rough stone or a grainy photo on a clean flat color; a photo cutout on a flat graphic.
techniques.use_when: Making material and craft felt; product shots; collage mixing photography and flat graphics.
techniques.fails_when: The background has its own texture or noise and competes.
techniques.foundation: Julesz, textons and texture segregation (1981)
techniques.distinct: Label it only when the texture change is what separates the subject from its ground. Dither, halftone and noise count as texture when they read as a surface. If the texture is there to show how the image was made, that's visible facture.

techniques.name: Selective focus
techniques.definition: Only the subject is sharp; everything around it is blurred.
techniques.why: Sharpness signals importance, so the eye settles on the sharp area and skips the blur.
techniques.spot: Shallow depth of field: a soft background or foreground and one sharp plane.
techniques.use_when: Close attention to one detail; separating a subject from a cluttered real setting; intimacy.
techniques.fails_when: Focus lands on the wrong thing, or the blur wipes out context the story needs.
techniques.foundation: Photographic depth of field

techniques.name: Glow
techniques.definition: An element seems to give off light: a bright core fading softly into darker surroundings.
techniques.why: A soft gradient around a bright center makes the eye read it as a light source, so it outshines everything that only reflects light.
techniques.spot: Neon, backlit halos, screens and orbs glowing on dark, light leaking around a subject.
techniques.use_when: Energy, technology, the sacred, night; making one element the source of attention.
techniques.fails_when: Everything glows, or the glow muddies edges and text.
techniques.distinct: Rim light is a thin edge from behind; chiaroscuro models form with light falling on it; glow is light that seems to come from the thing itself. Tie-breaker with chiaroscuro and glow: when the light comes from a direction and models the form, it is chiaroscuro; when the figure is the brightest thing in the picture with no visible source, it is glow.
techniques.foundation: Zavagno, the glare effect (1999)

techniques.name: Exaggeration
techniques.definition: The defining feature pushed beyond reality: huge eyes, a stretched limb, an enormous product, a caricatured face.
techniques.why: We recognize things by what sets them apart; pushing that difference further makes recognition faster and memory stronger.
techniques.spot: Proportions no real body or object has, distorted in the direction of the subject's most typical trait.
techniques.use_when: Character design, caricature, mascots, product hero shots, satire.
techniques.fails_when: The wrong trait is pushed, so the subject becomes less recognizable instead of more.
techniques.foundation: Ramachandran & Hirstein, the peak shift principle, The Science of Art (1999)

techniques.name: Isolation in void
techniques.definition: The subject alone in a large empty space.
techniques.why: With nothing to compete with, the single object gets all the attention, and the emptiness adds weight and calm.
techniques.spot: A small or medium subject in a big plain field, usually with more than half the frame left empty.
techniques.use_when: Luxury, focus, solitude, one idea or one product; quiet editorial pages.
techniques.fails_when: The empty space gets filled with logos and copy later, or the subject is too small to read.
techniques.distinct: Center placement is about position on the axis; isolation is about the emptiness around the subject, centered or not.
techniques.foundation: Ma, the meaningful interval in Japanese aesthetics; von Restorff's isolation effect (1933)

techniques.name: Center placement
techniques.definition: The subject placed dead center, often frontal, so it becomes the still heart of the image.
techniques.why: People tend to look at the center of an image first, and a centered subject reads as important, stable and direct.
techniques.spot: Subject on the central axis, even margins, little competing around it.
techniques.use_when: Icons, portraits with authority, product heroes, confrontation, ceremony.
techniques.fails_when: The image needs movement or story; centering then feels static or stiff.
techniques.foundation: Arnheim, The Power of the Center (1982); Tatler, the central fixation bias (2007)

techniques.name: Frame within a frame
techniques.definition: A doorway, window, mirror, screen or cut-out frames the subject a second time inside the picture.
techniques.why: The inner frame isolates the subject and adds depth: the eye passes through the outer layer into the inner one.
techniques.spot: Subject seen through a door, window, arch, mirror, screen or shaped opening.
techniques.use_when: Intimacy or voyeurism, focus, a story inside a story, layered depth.
techniques.fails_when: The inner frame is weak or cut off, or the frame is more interesting than what it holds.
techniques.foundation: Painting and film composition, e.g. the doorway view in Vermeer's The Love Letter (c. 1669)

techniques.name: Split comparison
techniques.definition: One frame divided to show with and without, before and after, or two options side by side, the same in everything except what is being compared.
techniques.why: When everything else is held equal, the single difference is impossible to miss.
techniques.spot: Half-and-half images, with and without a filter or product, A versus B layouts.
techniques.use_when: Proving an effect, product demonstrations, research comparisons.
techniques.fails_when: Other things change between the halves too, so the comparison is muddy.
techniques.distinct: Temporal synthesis compresses several moments of one process; a split comparison sets two states side by side to compare them.
techniques.foundation: Tufte on keeping comparisons within one glance, Envisioning Information (1990)

techniques.name: Pattern break
techniques.definition: A regular pattern (a grid, a row, a rhythm) with one element that breaks the rule.
techniques.why: Repetition sets up an expectation, and the single violation gets noticed and remembered.
techniques.spot: Rows of identical items with one turned, missing, out of line, or replaced by a different kind of thing.
techniques.use_when: Be-the-exception messages; standing out in a category; showing the anomaly.
techniques.fails_when: The pattern isn't regular enough to set an expectation, so the break doesn't register.
techniques.distinct: Pop-out changes one feature of one item; a pattern break breaks the arrangement itself or swaps in a different kind of thing.
techniques.foundation: von Restorff, the isolation effect (1933)

techniques.name: Direct gaze
techniques.definition: A face or eye (human, animal or drawn) looking straight out, meeting the viewer's eyes.
techniques.why: Eye contact is detected fast and holds attention, and it makes the viewer feel addressed.
techniques.spot: Eyes aimed at the lens, often the only face looking out while others look away.
techniques.use_when: Confrontation, intimacy, testimony, a call to act; covers and portraits.
techniques.fails_when: Every face looks out so none stands out, or the eyes are too small or shadowed to read.
techniques.distinct: A gaze cue looks at something inside the picture and sends your eye there; a direct gaze looks at you.
techniques.foundation: von Grünau & Anston, the stare-in-the-crowd effect (1995)

techniques.name: Semantic contrast
techniques.definition: Two things with opposite meanings put together so each sharpens the other: life and death, luxury and trash, nature and machine.
techniques.why: Placed side by side, opposites force a comparison, and the clash is the message.
techniques.spot: A pairing that feels charged or wrong: a gas mask on a bride, a flower in a rifle barrel, healthy forest beside a clear-cut.
techniques.use_when: Provocation, consequence, before and after, irony, cause campaigns.
techniques.fails_when: The opposition is too subtle to read, or so obvious it says nothing new.
techniques.distinct: Side-by-side analogy pairs things for their likeness; semantic contrast pairs them for their opposition.
techniques.foundation: Phillips & McQuarrie, juxtaposition for opposition, typology of visual rhetoric (2004); Barthes, Rhetoric of the Image (1964)

techniques.name: Highlight and mute
techniques.definition: In a chart, diagram or block of text, the one series, point or phrase that matters gets the color or full ink; everything else goes gray.
techniques.why: Muting the context makes the story line the first thing the eye finds, while the rest stays available for comparison.
techniques.spot: Gray lines or bars with one in a strong color; a headline set mostly in gray with the key words in full ink.
techniques.use_when: One finding must stand out among many; explanatory charts; research visuals that make one claim.
techniques.fails_when: Several things are highlighted, or the muted context is so faint it can't be read.
techniques.foundation: Knaflic, Storytelling with Data (2015); Treisman & Gelade (1980)
techniques.distinct: Use the Feature path for text and interfaces, the Encoding path for charts and diagrams. One word in color with the rest in plain white or black counts too, as long as the rest is uniformly quiet. Saturation accent is the same move in a picture. Two-tone headlines count only when the emphasized part is the key phrase. Weight alone counts too: bold key words in a light sentence.

techniques.name: Common baseline
techniques.definition: Values compared as positions or lengths on one shared scale, so differences can be read precisely.
techniques.why: People judge position along a common scale more accurately than angle, area or color.
techniques.spot: Aligned bars, dot plots, values on one axis instead of pies, bubbles or color shades.
techniques.use_when: Small differences matter; the reader must compare exactly; honest evidence.
techniques.fails_when: Baselines differ between parts (stacked middles, broken axes), so comparisons quietly mislead.
techniques.foundation: Cleveland & McGill, Graphical Perception (1984)

techniques.name: Color scale
techniques.definition: A data value mapped to color along a ramp (light to dark, or two colors meeting at a midpoint), as in heatmaps and choropleth maps.
techniques.why: Ordered lightness reads as more and less, so patterns across a whole field show at a glance.
techniques.spot: Heatmaps, choropleths, gradients keyed to a legend, fractals colored by iteration count.
techniques.use_when: Patterns across many cells, geography, density.
techniques.fails_when: A rainbow ramp invents boundaries the data doesn't have, or lightness doesn't follow the order.
techniques.distinct: Count it only when lightness or a two-color ramp reads as more and less. A rainbow of iterations is decoration unless it carries order. Categorical hue gives each kind its own color with no order.
techniques.foundation: Bertin, Sémiologie graphique (1967); Harrower & Brewer, ColorBrewer (2003)

techniques.name: Color blocking
techniques.definition: Large flat fields of solid color organize the image; everything sharing a color reads as one zone, even when far apart.
techniques.why: Shared features bind things together: similar color, shape or texture is grouped before it is read.
techniques.spot: Bold flat color areas, outfits or objects matched to their backgrounds, color used to sort parts into sets.
techniques.use_when: A product family, a system, a set that should read as one; fashion and editorial layouts.
techniques.fails_when: Too many colors, so the blocks no longer sort anything.
techniques.foundation: Wertheimer, the law of similarity (1923)
techniques.distinct: Color blocking groups through flat fields of color; for any other shared treatment (palette, texture, shape language), use similarity.

techniques.name: Similarity
techniques.definition: Different elements share one treatment (palette, shape language, texture, frame or type), so they read as one family.
techniques.why: Shared features bind things into groups before they are read one by one.
techniques.spot: Brand boards, product families, a series with one consistent finish, diagram parts coded by a shared color.
techniques.use_when: Systems, campaigns, sets that must read as one.
techniques.fails_when: The shared trait is too weak against the differences between items.
techniques.distinct: Color blocking groups through flat color fields; repetition repeats the same unit; similarity binds different units through a shared treatment.
techniques.foundation: Wertheimer, the law of similarity (1923)

techniques.name: Value massing
techniques.definition: The image organized into a few large shapes of dark and light, so it reads at a glance as one strong pattern.
techniques.why: Merging many parts into a few value masses simplifies the picture into a structure the eye grasps instantly.
techniques.spot: Big flat blacks against white (spotted blacks in ink and manga), a figure and its shadow merged into one dark shape.
techniques.use_when: Posters, ink illustration, manga, logos; impact from far away.
techniques.fails_when: Mid-tones break the masses into many small pieces.
techniques.distinct: Chiaroscuro models one subject with light; value massing designs the whole picture as a few flat lights and darks.
techniques.foundation: Notan, brought into Western design teaching by Arthur Wesley Dow, Composition (1899)

techniques.name: Proximity
techniques.definition: Elements placed close together read as one group, separate from elements further away.
techniques.why: The eye binds near things into units before reading them one by one.
techniques.spot: Clear clusters, with bigger gaps between clusters than inside them.
techniques.use_when: Organizing many items into a few understandable sets: layouts, product families, data clusters.
techniques.fails_when: Gaps inside groups are as large as the gaps between them.
techniques.foundation: Wertheimer, laws of perceptual organization (1923)

techniques.name: Repetition
techniques.definition: The same element repeated many times, so the set reads as one pattern with its own rhythm.
techniques.why: Repeated identical units fuse into a texture or a row, and the repetition itself becomes the image.
techniques.spot: Grids or rows of the same object, face, product or mark.
techniques.use_when: Abundance, mass production, a system, insistence; setting up a pattern to break.
techniques.fails_when: The units vary too much to fuse, or the repetition has no point and reads as wallpaper.
techniques.foundation: Wertheimer, the law of similarity (1923)
techniques.distinct: Repetition is the same unit side by side; self-similarity is the same form nested inside itself at smaller scales; similarity binds different units through a shared treatment.

techniques.name: Common region
techniques.definition: Elements inside the same container (a box, card, panel, color field or outline) read as a group, even when far apart.
techniques.why: A shared boundary overrides distance and similarity in deciding what belongs together.
techniques.spot: Cards, panels, boxes, tinted areas or outlines holding sets of items.
techniques.use_when: Interface layouts, product sets, separating sections without drawing lines.
techniques.fails_when: The containers are so many and so alike that each item just sits alone in its own box, or boxes nest so deep that nothing groups.
techniques.foundation: Palmer, Common Region (1992)
techniques.distinct: Bento grids count when each cell groups the things inside it (a stat with its label, an image with its caption). Proximity groups by distance alone; common region groups by a shared container.

techniques.name: Connection
techniques.definition: Lines, threads or paths physically link elements, so linked things read as one structure.
techniques.why: Connected elements are seen as a unit, strongly enough to override distance and color.
techniques.spot: Node-and-line diagrams, strings, cables, roads, flowcharts, constellations.
techniques.use_when: Relationships, networks, systems, cause and effect.
techniques.fails_when: So many crossing links that the structure turns into a tangle.
techniques.foundation: Palmer & Rock, uniform connectedness (1994)
techniques.distinct: Use the Encoding path when the links carry data (a network or flow diagram), the Gestalt path when they're compositional.

techniques.name: Good continuation
techniques.definition: Elements arranged along a smooth line or curve read as one continuous path, and the eye follows it.
techniques.why: We prefer smooth, unbroken contours, so aligned parts are seen as one line.
techniques.spot: Objects lined up on an invisible curve; a path, river or row that bends through the frame.
techniques.use_when: Tying separate parts into one flow; leading toward a product; graceful compositions.
techniques.fails_when: Gaps or sharp angles break the line so it reads as separate pieces.
techniques.distinct: Leading lines are actual lines in the scene pointing at a subject; good continuation is the eye joining separate elements into one line.
techniques.foundation: Wertheimer (1923)

techniques.name: Symmetry
techniques.definition: Elements mirrored around an axis, so the two halves read as one balanced whole.
techniques.why: Symmetric arrangements are seen as single, complete figures, and they feel stable, formal and deliberate.
techniques.spot: Mirror-image layouts, a central axis, frontal architecture and faces.
techniques.use_when: Authority, ceremony, calm, perfection; logos and emblems.
techniques.fails_when: Near-symmetry looks like a mistake, or symmetry is used where tension is needed.
techniques.foundation: Koffka, Principles of Gestalt Psychology (1935)

techniques.name: Self-similarity
techniques.definition: The same form nested inside itself at smaller and smaller scales: fractals, branching, spirals of spirals.
techniques.why: One rule generating every scale makes the whole read as a single system, and suggests it goes on forever.
techniques.spot: Fractal renders, trees and rivers branching, recursive layouts.
techniques.use_when: Growth, nature, infinity, complexity from a simple rule.
techniques.fails_when: The levels don't visibly share the form, so it reads as noise.
techniques.distinct: Repetition is the same unit side by side; self-similarity is the same form inside itself.
techniques.foundation: Mandelbrot, The Fractal Geometry of Nature (1982)

techniques.name: Face schema
techniques.definition: Unrelated elements arranged so they read as a face: two dots and a line, a car front, a power outlet.
techniques.why: We are wired to find faces in the simplest configurations, and once seen, the face holds the parts together.
techniques.spot: Objects, layouts or marks whose placement suggests eyes and a mouth.
techniques.use_when: Making objects friendly or alive; mascots, packaging, playful logos.
techniques.fails_when: The face is too faint to notice, or appears by accident where it undermines the message.
techniques.foundation: Face pareidolia; Johnson & Morton, Biology and Cognitive Development: The Case of Face Recognition (1991)
techniques.distinct: Decide by how it reads. If the parts read first as something else (a car front, an outlet, a layout) and a face emerges from them, it's face schema. If it reads first as a character with a face, it's anthropomorphism.

techniques.name: Small multiples
techniques.definition: The same small chart or image repeated in a grid, each panel showing one slice: a year, a place, a category.
techniques.why: Identical frames fuse into one set, so the eye ignores the frame and compares only what changes.
techniques.spot: A grid of same-size, same-scale mini charts, maps or photos.
techniques.use_when: Comparing across many categories, change over time, variants in a series.
techniques.fails_when: Scales differ between panels, or panels are too small to read.
techniques.foundation: Tufte, Envisioning Information (1990)
techniques.distinct: Small multiples compare slices of one measure in a shared frame. A grid of pictures that isn't comparing anything (a character lookbook, a type weight ladder) is similarity or repetition instead.

techniques.name: Direct labeling
techniques.definition: Labels sit right on or beside the marks they name, instead of in a separate legend.
techniques.why: Nearness binds the label to its mark, so the reader never has to look back and forth.
techniques.spot: Series names at line ends, values on bars, names on map regions, no legend box.
techniques.use_when: Any chart that must be read quickly or by non-specialists.
techniques.fails_when: Labels collide or cover the data.
techniques.foundation: Tufte, The Visual Display of Quantitative Information (1983); Wertheimer on proximity (1923)
techniques.distinct: Direct labeling names a mark; annotation adds a takeaway or an interpretation.

techniques.name: Categorical hue
techniques.definition: Each category or series gets its own hue, so everything of one kind can be followed across a chart or diagram.
techniques.why: Distinct hues separate categories without implying an order, and same-hue marks group across distance.
techniques.spot: Multi-series line charts, colored node types in a network, legend-keyed categories.
techniques.use_when: Comparing a handful of categories; following series through a dense chart.
techniques.fails_when: More than six or seven hues, or hues that differ only slightly.
techniques.distinct: A color scale implies more and less; categorical hue only says 'different kind'.
techniques.foundation: Bertin, Sémiologie graphique (1967)

techniques.name: Common fate
techniques.definition: Elements that move together, in the same direction and at the same speed, read as one group.
techniques.why: Shared motion binds things more strongly than looking alike.
techniques.spot: In motion: particles, flocks or interface parts moving as one. In stills: blur or streaks pointing the same way.
techniques.use_when: Showing that separate things act as one system; transitions that regroup elements.
techniques.fails_when: Too many groups move at once, or the motion is too subtle to notice.
techniques.foundation: Wertheimer, common fate (1923)

techniques.name: Size hierarchy
techniques.definition: Elements graded by size and weight, so they are read biggest first, then down the ranks.
techniques.why: Larger and heavier elements are seen first, so a clear ladder of sizes becomes a reading order.
techniques.spot: Headline, subhead, body; a large lead image with smaller supporting ones.
techniques.use_when: Any layout with more than one message: posters, editorial pages, interfaces.
techniques.fails_when: Too many similar sizes, so no clear order emerges.
techniques.foundation: Müller-Brockmann, Grid Systems in Graphic Design (1981)

techniques.name: Leading lines
techniques.definition: Lines in the scene (roads, rails, edges, arms, shadows), or drawn lines radiating toward it, point to the subject.
techniques.why: The eye travels along lines and edges to where they converge.
techniques.spot: Converging perspective lines, diagonals that end at the subject, paths into the frame.
techniques.use_when: Pulling the eye to something small or far away; depth; a sense of journey.
techniques.fails_when: Lines lead out of the frame or to empty space, taking attention with them.
techniques.foundation: Zettl, graphic vectors, Sight Sound Motion (1973)
techniques.distinct: Manga focus lines, drawn radiating toward the subject, count as leading lines. A pointer is a sign (an arrow, a cursor); leading lines are part of the scene or its drawing. Tie-breaker with halo framing: rays or rings that radiate from a central figure and frame it are halo framing; lines that converge on a subject somewhere else are leading lines. Never label the same rays as both.

techniques.name: Depth layering
techniques.definition: Clear foreground, middle ground and background planes that the eye moves through, near to far.
techniques.why: Overlap and size cues stack the image into planes, and we read them in order of distance.
techniques.spot: A foreground element framing or partly covering the scene (a branch, a shoulder, a railing), then the subject, then the distance.
techniques.use_when: Immersion, scale, a sense of being inside the scene.
techniques.fails_when: The foreground is so strong it steals the subject's attention.
techniques.foundation: Repoussoir in landscape painting; Zettl (1973)
techniques.distinct: Distance shown by planes fading into haze or fog (aerial perspective) counts too. Occlusion is one thing hiding another; depth layering is the whole scene stepping back in planes.

techniques.name: Gaze cue
techniques.definition: A figure looks at something in the image, and the viewer's eye follows the look.
techniques.why: Seeing someone look somewhere shifts our own attention there almost automatically.
techniques.spot: Faces or eyes turned toward a product, a headline or another person.
techniques.use_when: Directing attention to text or a product; story between characters.
techniques.fails_when: The gaze points away from what matters, or out of the frame.
techniques.distinct: A direct gaze looks at the viewer; a gaze cue looks at something in the picture. A figure seen from behind, looking into the scene so that we look with them, is a viewer stand-in.
techniques.foundation: Friesen & Kingstone, gaze cueing (1998)

techniques.name: Body vector
techniques.definition: Pointing arms, leaning bodies and directions of movement lead the eye along their line.
techniques.why: We read bodies as having direction, and follow where a gesture or posture aims.
techniques.spot: Outstretched arms, pointing fingers, running or leaning figures, a dancer's line.
techniques.use_when: Energy, action, steering attention through a scene.
techniques.fails_when: Gestures point in many directions and cancel each other out.
techniques.foundation: Zettl, index vectors (1973); Arnheim (1954)
techniques.distinct: Body vector is where a pose sends the eye; implied motion is a still reading as moving. One striding figure can do both; label both only if each does real work.

techniques.name: Reading path
techniques.definition: The layout follows the reader's learned direction: top left to bottom right in Latin scripts, right to left in manga.
techniques.why: Reading habits steer the eye even in images, so placing elements along that route sets the order they are met.
techniques.spot: Z or F shaped layouts, a story laid out left to right, manga pages read right to left.
techniques.use_when: Before and after, cause and effect, multi-step stories; any page with an order of reading.
techniques.fails_when: The order of information fights the reading direction, like the after placed before the before.
techniques.foundation: Arnold, the Gutenberg diagram (newspaper design); Nielsen, the F-shaped reading pattern (2006)

techniques.name: Pointer
techniques.definition: A drawn arrow, cursor, tail or line points at something, so the eye goes there next.
techniques.why: Arrows are learned signs, but we follow them almost as automatically as a gaze.
techniques.spot: Arrows, cursors, tooltip tails, leader lines that point rather than label.
techniques.use_when: Interfaces, explainers, step-by-step diagrams.
techniques.fails_when: Too many arrows compete, or they point at nothing important.
techniques.distinct: Gaze cues and body vectors point with people, leading lines with the scene; a pointer is a sign added to point.
techniques.foundation: Tipples, orienting to uninformative arrows (2002)

techniques.name: Layering and separation
techniques.definition: Data drawn in strong ink and structure (grids, axes, frames) in faint ink, so the eye reads the data first.
techniques.why: Contrast sorts the image into layers, and the faintest layer is read last, or only when needed.
techniques.spot: Light gray gridlines, thin axes, bold data marks.
techniques.use_when: Dense charts and diagrams; maps; any image with scaffolding.
techniques.fails_when: Gridlines and frames are as heavy as the data, so everything competes.
techniques.foundation: Tufte, Envisioning Information (1990)

techniques.name: Annotation
techniques.definition: Short notes placed on the chart at the moment that matters, telling the reader where to look and what it means.
techniques.why: A note in the right spot sets both the order of reading and the takeaway.
techniques.spot: Callouts with leader lines, labeled events on a timeline, a sentence beside a peak.
techniques.use_when: Explanatory charts for non-experts; research visuals that make one claim.
techniques.fails_when: Too many notes, or notes that repeat what the chart already shows.
techniques.foundation: Segel & Heer, Narrative Visualization (2010)
techniques.distinct: Direct labeling names a mark; annotation adds a takeaway or an interpretation.

techniques.name: Temporal synthesis
techniques.definition: Several moments compressed into one image: multiple exposures, motion trails, stroboscopic sequences, before and after in one frame.
techniques.why: Seeing stages side by side lets the eye read change as a sequence inside a still picture.
techniques.spot: Repeated ghosted figures, step-by-step poses in one frame, a split scene showing two times.
techniques.use_when: Showing process, growth, motion, cause and effect.
techniques.fails_when: The stages overlap so much they can't be told apart.
techniques.foundation: Marey's chronophotography (1880s)
techniques.distinct: Temporal synthesis compresses several moments of one process; a split comparison sets two states side by side to compare them.

techniques.name: Staging
techniques.definition: One idea presented at a time, posed and timed so it cannot be missed before the next begins.
techniques.why: Attention handles one clear action at a time; staging removes competition across time, the way isolation does across space.
techniques.spot: In motion: one element moves while the others hold still, clear poses, pauses before the next beat.
techniques.use_when: Animated explainers, interface transitions, character animation.
techniques.fails_when: Several things move at once and the eye doesn't know where to go.
techniques.foundation: Thomas & Johnston, The Illusion of Life (1981)

techniques.name: Progressive reveal
techniques.definition: Information appears in steps (build animations, scroll reveals, layers switched on), so the order of understanding is controlled.
techniques.why: Showing parts in sequence stops the viewer from reading everything at once and missing the argument.
techniques.spot: Charts that build series by series, diagrams that assemble, text that arrives line by line.
techniques.use_when: Explaining a complex system or argument; presentations; research animations.
techniques.fails_when: Each step is too slow, or the final full picture is never shown.
techniques.foundation: Progressive disclosure in interface design (Nielsen, 2006); Segel & Heer (2010)

techniques.name: Panel rhythm
techniques.definition: In comics and manga, the size, number and spacing of panels control how fast or slow time passes.
techniques.why: Readers linger on wide, empty panels and rush through rows of small ones, so the page layout becomes the clock.
techniques.spot: A full-page splash after small fast panels; long horizontal panels for silence; tight grids for action.
techniques.use_when: Manga and comics pacing; storyboards; any sequential layout.
techniques.fails_when: Every panel is the same size, so the story has no tempo.
techniques.foundation: McCloud, Understanding Comics (1993)

techniques.name: Closure
techniques.definition: An incomplete shape that the viewer completes: an outline with gaps, a form implied by fragments or by the space around it.
techniques.why: The mind fills gaps to make whole, simple forms, and that small effort makes the image stick.
techniques.spot: Logos and illustrations with missing lines that still read as complete; shapes implied by the marks around them.
techniques.use_when: Memorable marks, minimal logos, involving the viewer.
techniques.fails_when: Too much is missing, so the form can't be completed.
techniques.foundation: Gestalt closure; Kanizsa's illusory contours (1955)
techniques.distinct: Density emergence is a complete form built up from many marks (string art, point clouds): nothing is missing for the viewer to fill in, so it isn't closure.

techniques.name: Figure-ground reversal
techniques.definition: An image with two readings, depending on which part you see as the shape and which as the background.
techniques.why: The eye can hold only one figure at a time, and discovering the second reading gives a small jolt of reward.
techniques.spot: Negative-space forms: an arrow between letters, two faces that are also a vase, an animal hidden in the gap.
techniques.use_when: Clever logos, double meanings, posters that reward a second look.
techniques.fails_when: The hidden shape is too hard to find, or the main reading collapses.
techniques.foundation: Rubin, Synsoplevede Figurer (1915)

techniques.name: Crop at the edge
techniques.definition: The subject is cut by the frame, so the viewer completes it outside the picture.
techniques.why: A cropped form keeps going in the mind, adding tension, movement and a sense of a larger world.
techniques.spot: Faces, bodies or objects cut by the frame edge, often off center.
techniques.use_when: Intimacy, motion, scale, a feeling that the moment continues beyond the image.
techniques.fails_when: The crop removes what identifies the subject, or looks accidental.
techniques.foundation: Degas's cropped compositions, shaped by Japanese prints and photography
techniques.distinct: Not every close-up: only crops that add tension or scale, or make the scene feel like it continues past the frame. Frame break is the opposite: the subject crosses the frame and comes toward us instead of being cut by it.

techniques.name: Occlusion
techniques.definition: One thing partly hides another, and the viewer completes what is hidden.
techniques.why: We automatically complete objects behind others, and filling in makes the hidden part feel present and charged.
techniques.spot: Faces behind hands, objects behind veils or edges, things peeking out from behind something.
techniques.use_when: Mystery, modesty, teasing a reveal, depth.
techniques.fails_when: So much is hidden that the subject can't be identified.
techniques.foundation: Michotte, amodal completion (1964)

techniques.name: Forced perspective
techniques.definition: Objects placed at different distances so they seem to touch or interact at an impossible scale.
techniques.why: Without clear depth cues the eye reads size relations at face value, and the false relation becomes the idea.
techniques.spot: A person holding up a building, a giant hand in the foreground, a tiny figure on a huge object.
techniques.use_when: Playful surprise, product as hero, scale jokes.
techniques.fails_when: The trick shows (misaligned contact points, mismatched focus), so it reads as fake.
techniques.foundation: Trick photography and film practice

techniques.name: Transparency
techniques.definition: A layer reads as glass, film or water because of how it bends, tints or blurs what is behind it.
techniques.why: When the colors and edges behind a surface shift in a consistent way, the eye infers a see-through layer and its material.
techniques.spot: Frosted glass panels, refraction distortions, translucent overlapping shapes, water surfaces.
techniques.use_when: Layered interfaces, material and depth without shadow, softness.
techniques.fails_when: What is behind the layer is too busy or too plain to show the effect.
techniques.foundation: Metelli, The Perception of Transparency (1974)

techniques.name: Anthropomorphism
techniques.definition: Objects, animals or brands given human traits: faces, gestures, posture, emotion.
techniques.why: We readily see minds and feelings in things that act human, and relate to them as characters.
techniques.spot: Objects with eyes or limbs, animals in human clothes or poses, products acting like people.
techniques.use_when: Making brands friendly, mascots, humor, empathy for non-human subjects.
techniques.fails_when: The human traits turn uncanny, or the object's own identity gets lost.
techniques.foundation: Epley, Waytz & Cacioppo, On Seeing Human (2007)
techniques.distinct: Decide by how it reads. A character that reads first as having a face or human manner is anthropomorphism; a face that emerges from parts that read first as something else is face schema.

techniques.name: Side-by-side analogy
techniques.definition: Two things placed next to each other so the viewer transfers the qualities of one to the other.
techniques.why: Pairing invites comparison, and when the likeness is clear, the meaning of one rubs off on the other.
techniques.spot: A product beside an animal, object or scene that shares its shape or quality.
techniques.use_when: Explaining a benefit without words; making the abstract concrete.
techniques.fails_when: The likeness isn't visible, so the pairing seems random.
techniques.distinct: Fusion merges the two into one form; an analogy keeps them separate.
techniques.foundation: Phillips & McQuarrie, juxtaposition for similarity (2004)

techniques.name: Fusion
techniques.definition: Two objects merged into one hybrid form, so both meanings arrive at once.
techniques.why: The impossible object stops the eye, and decoding its two halves delivers the idea.
techniques.spot: A lightbulb that is also a pear, a hand made of trees, a building that is also a face.
techniques.use_when: One striking concept; editorial illustration; posters.
techniques.fails_when: One half is unrecognizable, or the combination means nothing beyond its strangeness.
techniques.foundation: Phillips & McQuarrie, fusion (2004)
techniques.distinct: If both identities stay visible in one form, it's fusion; if one object is absent and only its shape survives in another object's place, it's form substitution. Label invented hybrids where the merge is the idea; established creatures (a griffin, a mermaid, a harpy) are subjects, not fusion, unless the image makes the merge itself the point.

techniques.name: Form substitution
techniques.definition: An expected object is replaced by another of similar shape (a cigarette drawn as a bullet, a road as a ribbon), and the swap carries the meaning.
techniques.why: The familiar shape lets the eye accept the replacement; then the mind notices the swap and connects the two meanings.
techniques.spot: Something sitting where a different, similarly shaped thing belongs.
techniques.use_when: Warnings, wit, condensing a message into one image.
techniques.fails_when: The shapes are not similar enough for the swap to read at first glance.
techniques.distinct: If both identities stay visible in one form, it's fusion; if one object is absent and only its shape survives in another object's place, it's form substitution.
techniques.foundation: Phillips & McQuarrie, replacement (2004)

techniques.name: Contextual metaphor
techniques.definition: An ordinary object or small scene placed in a setting or story that gives it a new meaning: sneakers on a winner's podium, a tie hung like a noose, mice raiding the cheese.
techniques.why: The setting switches on a familiar script, and the object is read through it.
techniques.spot: The objects are unchanged; the situation or little story around them does the work.
techniques.use_when: Saying something about a product or idea without altering it; dry wit.
techniques.fails_when: The setting is too unfamiliar for the script to fire.
techniques.distinct: In form substitution the object changes; in a contextual metaphor only its surroundings do.
techniques.foundation: Phillips & McQuarrie, replacement (2004); Barthes, Rhetoric of the Image (1964)

techniques.name: Anchorage
techniques.definition: Words fix how the picture is read: a headline or caption picks which of the image's possible meanings counts.
techniques.why: Images are open to many readings; a line of text closes them down to one, and the pairing becomes the idea.
techniques.spot: A picture whose meaning turns on its caption, like 'Sensitive dependencies' over a butterfly; headlines that reframe an ordinary photo.
techniques.use_when: Campaigns, editorial, research visuals where the image must mean one thing.
techniques.fails_when: The text just repeats the picture, or contradicts it to no purpose.
techniques.distinct: Annotation explains data at a point; anchorage decides what a whole picture means.
techniques.foundation: Barthes, anchorage in Rhetoric of the Image (1964)

techniques.name: Genre quotation
techniques.definition: The image borrows the codes of a recognizable genre (film noir, pulp cover, propaganda poster, scientific plate, fashion cover) so its content is read through that genre.
techniques.why: Genre codes carry ready-made associations, so the borrowed look brings its meaning along.
techniques.spot: Typography, layout, color and photography that clearly belong to another kind of artifact.
techniques.use_when: Instant tone; irony; positioning something against a known reference.
techniques.fails_when: The audience doesn't know the genre, or the borrowing is pure costume with nothing to say.
techniques.distinct: Count it only when the borrowed genre is foreign to the artifact (a T-shirt dressed as an x-ray, a brand page dressed as a museum label). An artifact in its own category's look, like a science brand that looks scientific, is not quoting. Visual quotation cites one specific famous image.
techniques.foundation: Genette, Palimpsests (1982), on pastiche

techniques.name: Visual quotation
techniques.definition: A specific famous image (a pose, painting, film frame or photograph) recreated or referenced, so its meaning transfers.
techniques.why: Recognizing the original adds a second layer: the new image is read against the one it cites.
techniques.spot: A recognizable composition or pose restaged with new subjects.
techniques.use_when: Homage, parody, borrowing authority or nostalgia.
techniques.fails_when: The original is not recognized, or the quote is used without adding anything.
techniques.foundation: Kristeva, intertextuality (late 1960s)

techniques.name: Visible facture
techniques.definition: The traces of a process are left visible and carry meaning: brush strokes, construction lines, print misregistration, halftone and dither, compression glitches, torn edges.
techniques.why: Traces of making say how the image came to be (by hand, by a press, by a machine, by something breaking), and that becomes part of its meaning.
techniques.spot: Expressive brushwork, visible sketch lines, halftone dots, riso misprints, datamosh and pixel corruption, paper texture.
techniques.use_when: Warmth, craft, authenticity, process, or machine-ness and decay; pushing back against slick digital polish.
techniques.fails_when: The trace is decoration with nothing to say, or it hides the subject.
techniques.foundation: Faktura in the Russian avant-garde (1910s)
techniques.distinct: Label it when the trace says something (handmade, printed, machine-made, broken), not just because the medium shows; every watercolor has washes. If the texture mainly separates figure from ground, it's texture against flat; if it borrows a medium's look to evoke another era or genre, it's genre quotation. Dots that build a form no outline draws are density emergence; dots that show how the image was printed or made are visible facture.

techniques.name: Arbitrary color
techniques.definition: A color that cannot be natural (green skin, a blue horse) used so the color itself carries the meaning or feeling.
techniques.why: An impossible color can't be read as description, so the viewer reads it as expression or symbol.
techniques.spot: Figures or things painted in colors they never have, consistently and on purpose.
techniques.use_when: Emotion, the uncanny, the spiritual, a strong signature palette.
techniques.fails_when: It looks like a color error rather than a choice.
techniques.distinct: A saturation accent picks one thing out; arbitrary color changes what the thing means. A whole image washed in one unnatural color counts when the tint carries the feeling (a blood-red night, a city gone green); an ordinary color grade, sepia or a duotone print does not. Tone on tone keeps a picture inside one color family by choice; label arbitrary color only when the hue itself is one the subject could not have and carries the meaning.
techniques.foundation: Fauvism (Matisse, 1905); Franz Marc's blue horses (1911)

techniques.name: Learned symbol
techniques.definition: A sign whose meaning comes from convention, not appearance: a heart, a cross, red for stop, a dove, a laurel.
techniques.why: Once learned, symbols are read instantly and carry large meanings in small marks.
techniques.spot: Icons and objects that stand for an idea rather than for themselves.
techniques.use_when: Fast communication, signage, iconography, layered meaning.
techniques.fails_when: The audience doesn't share the convention, or the symbol is a cliché that adds nothing.
techniques.foundation: Peirce's icon, index and symbol (late 19th century); Barthes, Mythologies (1957)
techniques.distinct: Label it only when a specific symbol's conventional meaning is how the image communicates: a heart for love, a crucifixion pose, a skull for death. Not for decorative iconography or diagram notation (arrows, valves, flowchart shapes). Small story scenes whose situation carries the meaning are contextual metaphors. In religious and esoteric art: label a symbol when it carries a meaning beyond the subject (the dove, Death's scythe, a cross between antlers); not when it only tells you who the subject is (Diana's crescent, a saint's halo, Orpheus's lyre).

techniques.name: Sound lettering
techniques.definition: Sound effects drawn as lettering that becomes part of the image: the shape, weight and size of the letters carry the noise.
techniques.why: Readers hear the drawn word, and its form adds force, speed and texture to a silent picture.
techniques.spot: Manga and comics sound effects, words that crack, wobble or explode with the action.
techniques.use_when: Comics and manga, playful editorial, packaging with attitude.
techniques.fails_when: The lettering competes with the drawing instead of joining it.
techniques.foundation: Comics practice; McCloud, Understanding Comics (1993)

techniques.name: Pictorial units
techniques.definition: Data counted with small pictures of the thing being counted: one figure stands for a thousand people.
techniques.why: The shape says what is counted and the repetition says how many, so the chart reads without a legend.
techniques.spot: Rows of identical icons standing for quantities.
techniques.use_when: Public-facing statistics; quantities people should feel rather than estimate.
techniques.fails_when: Icons are scaled up in size instead of repeated, so their area misleads.
techniques.foundation: Otto and Marie Neurath, Isotype (from the 1920s)

techniques.name: Gutter closure
techniques.definition: Two frames or panels shown in sequence, and the viewer imagines what happened between them.
techniques.why: Readers automatically connect consecutive images into one event, supplying the missing action.
techniques.spot: A raised fist in one panel and a fallen figure in the next; a cut that skips the action.
techniques.use_when: Comics and manga, storyboards, editing, before and after pairs.
techniques.fails_when: The gap is too big to bridge, so the sequence reads as unrelated images.
techniques.foundation: McCloud, closure, Understanding Comics (1993)

techniques.name: Implied motion
techniques.definition: A still image made to read as moving: speed lines, motion blur, frozen mid-action poses, things caught falling.
techniques.why: The visual system fills in the movement it expects from these cues.
techniques.spot: Manga speed lines, streaks, poses at the peak of an action, splashes frozen in the air.
techniques.use_when: Energy and action in stills; product dynamism; sport.
techniques.fails_when: The cues contradict each other, or the blur hides the subject.
techniques.foundation: Futurist painting (Balla, Dynamism of a Dog on a Leash, 1912); manga speed lines
techniques.distinct: Implied motion shows movement under way; a pregnant moment stops just before the outcome. Body vector is where a pose sends the eye.

techniques.name: Pregnant moment
techniques.definition: A single image caught just before the decisive action, so the viewer supplies what happens next.
techniques.why: The instant of greatest tension holds the before and the after at once, and the mind completes the action.
techniques.spot: A foot about to land, a glass about to fall, a hand reaching for the door.
techniques.use_when: Suspense, story in one frame, narrative illustration.
techniques.fails_when: The outcome isn't predictable enough to imagine, or the moment is already past.
techniques.distinct: Implied motion shows movement under way; the pregnant moment stops just before the outcome.
techniques.foundation: Lessing, Laocoön (1766)

techniques.name: Match cut
techniques.definition: A cut or transition between two different things that share a shape or motion, so they read as one continuous thing.
techniques.why: Continuity of shape across the cut makes the mind connect the two subjects and carry meaning from one to the other.
techniques.spot: In video: a round object becoming another round object, a gesture finished by a different subject. In stills: diptychs with matched shapes.
techniques.use_when: Transitions in motion work, connecting ideas, time jumps.
techniques.fails_when: The shapes or motions don't line up, so the cut feels arbitrary.
techniques.foundation: Film editing; the bone-to-satellite cut in Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968)

techniques.name: Viewpoint
techniques.definition: The eye placed unusually low, high or tilted, or part of the subject thrust at the lens, so the angle itself changes how big, powerful or close the subject feels.
techniques.why: We read size and power from where we stand: looking up makes a figure loom, looking down makes it small, and a hand foreshortened at the lens seems to reach out of the picture.
techniques.spot: Figures seen from below against the sky, scenes from above, a tilted horizon, a foot, fist or blade huge in the foreground.
techniques.use_when: Making a hero, product or threat dominant; making a figure feel small or watched; adding unease or energy.
techniques.fails_when: The angle is mild or arbitrary, so it reads as a framing accident rather than a choice.
techniques.distinct: Scale disparity compares sizes inside the picture; viewpoint changes how big the subject feels through where the eye stands. Forced perspective uses distance to fake a relation between two things.
techniques.foundation: Mandell & Shaw, camera angle and how people are judged (1973); Meyers-Levy & Peracchio, Getting an angle in advertising (1992)

techniques.name: Frame break
techniques.definition: Part of the subject crosses the edge of its own frame, panel, card or border, so it seems to step out of the picture toward the viewer.
techniques.why: A frame tells the eye where the picture ends; whatever crosses it reads as nearer than the picture and more alive than what stays inside.
techniques.spot: An arm or blade over a panel border, an illustration spilling past its card, a painted scene running onto its mount.
techniques.use_when: Making a character, product or idea burst out; depth in flat layouts; drama in comics and covers.
techniques.fails_when: Too many things break the frame, so the frame stops meaning anything.
techniques.distinct: Crop at the edge cuts the subject off so the viewer completes it outside; frame break lets it cross the frame and come closer. Frame within a frame keeps the subject inside a second frame.
techniques.foundation: Trompe-l'œil escapes from the frame (Pere Borrell del Caso, Escaping Criticism, 1874); breaking the panel in comics (McCloud, Understanding Comics, 1993)

techniques.name: Hidden image
techniques.definition: A second picture concealed inside the first: a landscape that is also a face, a crowd made of tiny figures, a figure painted faintly into a cloud. It reads one way at a glance and another on a closer look.
techniques.why: Once the eye finds the second reading it can't unsee it, and the discovery makes the viewer an accomplice.
techniques.spot: Heads composed of fruit or bodies, a profile in the rocks, textures that resolve into faces up close.
techniques.use_when: Rewarding a second look; mystery, surreal or esoteric themes; marks with a secret.
techniques.fails_when: The hidden picture is too faint to find, or so obvious it isn't hidden.
techniques.distinct: Figure-ground reversal flips which shape is figure and which is background; face schema is an accidental face in an object; a hidden image is a deliberate second picture built into the first.
techniques.foundation: Arcimboldo's composite heads (1560s–1590s); Dalí's double images (1930s); multistable perception in Gestalt psychology

techniques.name: Density emergence
techniques.definition: A form built up from many marks, lines or points that pile up into a shape no single mark draws: string-art envelopes, point clouds, attractor plots, forms that exist only as dot or character density.
techniques.why: The eye reads where marks crowd as solid and where they thin as edge, so thousands of lines become one curved surface.
techniques.spot: Straight lines whose crossings make a curve, particle shells, plots of millions of points, forms made of text or dots.
techniques.use_when: Generative and data art; a whole emerging from many parts; delicate volume without outlines.
techniques.fails_when: The marks are too sparse to fuse, or so dense the form flattens into a blot.
techniques.distinct: Closure asks the viewer to complete a gap; density emergence gives a complete form made by accumulation. Repetition repeats a unit you still see as a unit; here the units disappear into the form. Halftone and dot grids are visible facture when the dot texture is the trace of a process; density emergence when the dots build a form no outline draws. Stipple used only as shading inside an outlined drawing is not density emergence.
techniques.foundation: Gestalt grouping (Wertheimer, 1923); curve stitching, popularized by Mary Everest Boole (c. 1900)

techniques.name: Viewer stand-in
techniques.definition: A figure seen from behind, looking into the scene, so the viewer looks with them and takes their place (the Rückenfigur).
techniques.why: A turned back hides the face we would read and offers its point of view instead; we step into the figure and see what it sees.
techniques.spot: A small figure with its back to us facing a vast landscape, the sea, a doorway, a monster.
techniques.use_when: Immersion, awe, solitude, an invitation into a world; stories where the viewer should feel present.
techniques.fails_when: The figure is so large or detailed it becomes the subject, or turns enough that we read its face instead.
techniques.distinct: Gaze cue sends the eye to a target the figure looks at; a viewer stand-in puts the viewer in the figure's place. Direct gaze is the opposite: the figure looks out at us. First-person view goes one step further: no figure, only the viewer's own hands or feet in shot.
techniques.foundation: Caspar David Friedrich's Rückenfigur (Wanderer above the Sea of Fog, c. 1818); Koerner, Caspar David Friedrich and the Subject of Landscape (1990)

techniques.name: Rebus
techniques.definition: Small pictures stand in for words or sounds inside a line of text or a name, so the viewer reads the pictures as language.
techniques.why: Swapping a word for a picture slows reading for a moment, and the small puzzle makes the message stick.
techniques.spot: An eye for 'I', a heart for 'love', icons or emoji set into a sentence, a name spelled partly in pictures.
techniques.use_when: Playful campaigns, memorable logos and taglines, lively interface copy.
techniques.fails_when: The picture could be read as several words, or the line takes too long to decode.
techniques.distinct: Pictorial units count things with pictures; a rebus reads pictures as words. Anchorage uses words to fix a picture's meaning; a rebus uses pictures in place of words.
techniques.foundation: The rebus tradition; Paul Rand's Eye-Bee-M poster for IBM (1981); Milton Glaser's I ♥ NY (1977)

techniques.name: Word as image
techniques.definition: Lettering shaped, placed or broken so its form acts out what the word says: text massed into the shape it names, a word that cracks where it says 'break'.
techniques.why: Reading and seeing happen at once, so the meaning lands twice in the time of one.
techniques.spot: Calligrams, a word melting or glitching to match its meaning, a name drawn into the object it names.
techniques.use_when: Logotypes, titles and posters where one word has to carry the idea.
techniques.fails_when: The word stops being readable, or the effect is decoration that doesn't match the meaning.
techniques.distinct: Sound lettering draws sound effects into a scene; word as image makes any word act out its meaning. A rebus swaps words for pictures; word as image turns the word itself into the picture.
techniques.foundation: Apollinaire, Calligrammes (1918); Ji Lee, Word as Image (2011)

techniques.name: Size encoding
techniques.definition: A value shown by the size of a mark: bubble area, the width of a ribbon or line, the size of a symbol on a map.
techniques.why: Bigger reads as more at a glance, so size ranks values instantly, though exact areas are judged poorly.
techniques.spot: Bubble charts, Sankey flows, proportional symbols on maps, tree maps.
techniques.use_when: Showing rough magnitude and ranking at a glance across many items.
techniques.fails_when: Exact comparisons matter (area is judged less accurately than position or length), or marks overlap until they can't be read.
techniques.distinct: Common baseline compares values by position or length on one scale, more precisely; color scale maps values to color; size encoding maps them to area or width.
techniques.foundation: Bertin, Semiology of Graphics (1967); Cleveland & McGill, graphical perception (1984)

techniques.name: Halo framing
techniques.definition: Rings, rays, a nimbus or a radiating pattern behind a central figure that frame it and seem to shine from it at once.
techniques.why: Radial lines and rings all point to their center, so the figure in the middle is found first and seems to give off the radiance around it.
techniques.spot: Haloes and mandorlas, sunbursts behind a figure or product, concentric rings, rays fanning from a head.
techniques.use_when: Sacred or iconic presence, heroic portraits, product reveals, making one figure the center of a world.
techniques.fails_when: The pattern is busier than the figure, or the figure sits off its center.
techniques.distinct: Glow is light coming from the thing itself; halo framing is a drawn structure around it. Frame within a frame encloses the subject; halo framing radiates from it. A halo as a sign of holiness is also a learned symbol; label halo framing when its shape organizes the picture. Tie-breaker with leading lines: lines that converge on a subject elsewhere are leading lines. Glow and halo framing can both stand on one radiant element: glow for the light itself, halo framing for the drawn rings or rays that organize the picture around the center.
techniques.foundation: The nimbus and mandorla in religious art; Arnheim, The Power of the Center (1982)

techniques.name: First-person view
techniques.definition: The picture is taken from the viewer's own eyes: their hands, feet, lap or the thing they hold come into the frame from the bottom edge, so the viewer becomes the one in the scene.
techniques.why: Limbs cut by the lower edge at the angle we see our own are read as ours; the scene stops being looked at and starts being lived in.
techniques.spot: Hands holding a cup, a phone, a book or a weapon from below; feet up on a bed or a sofa; a laptop on a lap; game and POV camera shots.
techniques.use_when: Immersion, intimacy, everyday ritual, a product in use; making the viewer the protagonist.
techniques.fails_when: The limbs are posed or lit like someone else's, or so small that the frame reads as an ordinary still life.
techniques.distinct: Viewer stand-in shows a figure from behind that we step into; first-person view puts us in our own body, with only our limbs in shot. A hand that is itself the subject (a hand study, a product held up for the camera by a model) is not first-person view. Viewpoint is the camera's height or angle; first-person view is the camera at the viewer's eyes with the viewer's own body in frame.
techniques.foundation: The point-of-view shot in film (Branigan, Point of View in the Cinema, 1984); Lady in the Lake (1947), a whole film shot first-person

techniques.name: Value accent
techniques.definition: One light shape in an otherwise dark image, or one dark shape in an otherwise light one, so the odd value takes the eye without any color doing it.
techniques.why: Lightness contrast is read before hue; when everything sits in one key, the single shape outside it is found first.
techniques.spot: A white face inside a black hood, a pale figure in a night scene, a few black accents in a white room, one dark chair on a pale floor.
techniques.use_when: Singling out a subject in monochrome or near-monochrome work; quiet focus without color.
techniques.fails_when: Several shapes share the odd value, or the rest of the image isn't kept in one key.
techniques.distinct: Saturation accent does this with one vivid color; value accent does it with lightness alone, in any palette. Chiaroscuro models form with light and shadow across the whole image; value accent sets one shape apart by its value. Value massing organizes the whole image into a few big light and dark shapes; value accent is one small shape against one large key. Pop-out needs a crowd of similar items with one odd one. Glow is light coming off the thing, a bright core fading into its surroundings; value accent is a pale shape that stays a shape, with no light spreading from it. When light spreads, label glow.
techniques.foundation: Itten's light-dark contrast, The Art of Color (1961); Livingstone, Vision and Art: The Biology of Seeing (2002)

techniques.name: Graphic overlay
techniques.definition: A flat drawn or graphic layer laid over a finished picture (usually a photograph, also a painting, illustration or render) and kept visibly separate from it (line art, glyphs, grids, callouts, type), often lined up with a real feature so the two layers read together.
techniques.why: The eye takes the picture underneath as the world and the flat marks as a comment on it; where they line up, the drawing seems to reveal something hidden in it.
techniques.spot: Line art traced over a portrait, a sigil drawn on a landscape, circles and arrows annotating a photo, interface callouts floating over a face, doodles or a star grid laid over a painting, light ribbons drawn over an archive photo.
techniques.use_when: Annotation, revelation, hidden structure, mixing documentary and graphic registers, tech or occult overlays.
techniques.fails_when: The overlay melts into the picture (then it is retouching), ignores it so the two layers don't relate, or is drawn in the same hand and medium as the picture (then it is part of the drawing).
techniques.distinct: Collage cuts and joins pieces of different pictures; graphic overlay keeps one photo whole and draws on top of it. Transparency is a see-through material inside the scene; graphic overlay is a flat layer on the picture surface. Direct labeling names the marks of a chart; graphic overlay draws on a photograph. Text laid over a photo only as a caption or title is not graphic overlay unless it relates to what it covers.
techniques.foundation: Layering and separation in information design (Tufte, Envisioning Information, 1990); annotated and drawn-over photographs in photomontage
