techniques.name: Cast-light pattern
techniques.definition: Light falling through something outside the frame (blinds, a window grid, leaves, lace) lays a shaped pattern of light and shadow across the scene and the people in it.
techniques.why: A shaped patch of light implies its source and the space beyond the frame, and the stripes or dapples wrap over every surface they cross, binding the scene together.
techniques.spot: Venetian-blind stripes across a face or a wall, a window's squares on the floor, leaf dapple, a lace shadow on skin, late sun through a grille.
techniques.use_when: Mood and time of day, noir tension, warmth and stillness in interiors; implying a world outside the frame.
techniques.fails_when: The pattern is too faint to read as shaped light, or so busy it breaks up the subject.
techniques.distinct: Chiaroscuro models form with light and dark; a cast-light pattern is a shape thrown by light from an unseen source. Repetition repeats objects; here the repeated shape is the light itself. Glow is light coming from the thing; cast light comes from outside the frame.
techniques.foundation: Window and blind patterns in film noir lighting (the cookie, or cucoloris); Baxandall, Shadows and Enlightenment (1995)

techniques.name: Warped grid
techniques.definition: A regular grid or mesh bent out of true, so its distortion shows a force, a field or a curved surface that is otherwise invisible.
techniques.why: We know the grid should be straight and even, so every bend reads as something pushing on it; the deformation draws the invisible shape.
techniques.spot: Spacetime wells under a planet, gravity funnels, wireframe terrain, graph paper bulging around an object, a mesh warp in type.
techniques.use_when: Physics and cosmology, invisible forces, data surfaces, the pull or influence of one thing on its surroundings.
techniques.fails_when: The grid is too faint or irregular to read as once straight, or the warp is decoration and shows nothing.
techniques.distinct: Leading lines converge on a subject; a warped grid bends around a cause. Density emergence builds a form out of many marks; a warped grid shows a form by deforming a known regular structure. Depth layering stacks flat planes; a warped grid curves one.
techniques.foundation: D'Arcy Thompson's transformation grids, On Growth and Form (1917); embedding diagrams of curved spacetime (Misner, Thorne and Wheeler, Gravitation, 1973)

techniques.name: Tone on tone
techniques.definition: The whole image kept inside one color family, tints and shades of a single hue or its close neighbors, so nothing stands out by color and the picture reads as one calm whole.
techniques.why: With hue held still, the eye stops sorting by color; small shifts in lightness, material and light carry the interest, and the shared color reads as a single mood.
techniques.spot: Cream-on-cream and beige-and-oak rooms, an outfit in shades of one color, a poster in tints of one hue, a room washed in one lamp's color, near-monochrome film or anime frames.
techniques.use_when: Calm, softness, luxury and restraint; letting form, texture and light carry the picture; a quiet field that makes a later accent land.
techniques.fails_when: Something breaks the family hard enough to become an accent (then label the accent), the palette goes so flat that the forms disappear, or the single hue is only a process (an old sepia print, a duotone) rather than a choice that carries the image.
techniques.distinct: Saturation accent and value accent set one thing apart by color or lightness; tone on tone sets nothing apart. Arbitrary color is a hue the subject could not have; tone on tone is about how few hues the image allows, natural or not. Similarity binds separate items into a family through a shared treatment; tone on tone keeps one picture inside one color family. Value massing organizes light and dark into big shapes; tone on tone is about hue. Black-and-white images are not tone on tone: there is no hue to hold back.
techniques.foundation: Monochromatic and analogous harmonies (Itten, The Art of Color, 1961); American Tonalism (Corn, The Color of Mood: American Tonalism, 1880–1910, 1972); tone-on-tone styling in interiors and fashion

techniques.name: Implied presence
techniques.definition: No one is in the picture, but traces show that someone was just here or is about to come back (an unmade bed, a steaming cup, shoes kicked off, a coat on an empty chair, an outfit laid out in the shape of a body), so the viewer pictures the missing person.
techniques.why: We read objects as evidence of use; a dent in a pillow or a half-finished drink sets the mind to fill in the absent body and the moment just before.
techniques.spot: Unmade beds, a laptop and headphones left on the duvet, a half-drunk glass, slippers by the bed, a coat on an empty chair, a book left open, a shadow burned into a wall, an outfit laid flat in body order.
techniques.use_when: Intimacy, nostalgia, loneliness or loss; lived-in interiors; stories told after the fact; inviting the viewer to imagine the person.
techniques.fails_when: The objects are styled so neatly they read as a product shot, or nothing points to a person or a moment. A person in the frame, even a small one, makes it something else, unless the trace plainly belongs to someone else who is gone.
techniques.distinct: Viewer stand-in shows a figure from behind and first-person view shows the viewer's own body; implied presence shows no one at all, only traces. Pregnant moment freezes an action just before it resolves; implied presence shows the scene after the person has gone. Closure completes a missing part of a shape; implied presence completes a missing person from evidence. A sleeping pet alone doesn't count unless the scene around it points to the owner.
techniques.foundation: The empty-chair tradition in painting (Van Gogh, Gauguin's Chair, 1888); Barthes, Camera Lucida (1980), on the photograph as a trace of what has been
